excerpt: When I started working on streaming in Neuron AI, I thought it was the easy part of the framework. The model produces text, you forward it to the browser, the user watches the answer appear. Done. It took me months, a custom protocol, a TypeScript package, and a long look at a pricing page to admit I was wrong. This article is the story of that journey and of the tool that came out of it. IQ-Stream is a streaming server that does one job: it carries the tokens generated by a large language model (LLM) from your application backend to your users’ browsers in real time, using Server-Sent Events. If a browser loses its connection in the middle of an answer, it gets back every event it missed as soon as it reconnects. Your backend talks to it with plain HTTP requests, so it works with PHP and with any other language. I’ll start from the basics, because many of you are building your first agent right now and not everything here is obvious. If you already know why streaming matters and how it works in PHP, feel free to skip ahead to the section about the limits I found along the way. What streaming means in an AI application An LLM doesn’t write an answer all at once. It generates text in small pieces called tokens, roughly a word or a part of a word each, one after another. A long answer of a few thousand tokens can take from tens of seconds to more than a minute to complete. If your application waits for the whole thing before showing anything, the user stares at a spinner for that entire time. Streaming means sending each piece to the browser as soon as the model produces it, so the user starts reading immediately. With agents, there’s more than text to stream. An agent can reason before answering, decide to call a tool (a PHP function that queries your database or calls an external API), wait for the result, and then continue writing.
